investigacion.base:
**Where things stand on Oct 18–19, 2026:** the count is **about 22 named storms**. One more storm, which would be named Vance, looks likely to form before Oct 29.

**Resolution sources**
- **Wikipedia "2026 Pacific hurricane season":** My search didn't show the "Total storms" number in the infobox, so you should check it directly. The article says this season has produced the highest accumulated cyclone energy value on record in the basin, surpassing the 2018 season, with ACE at 343.1.
- **Metaculus FAQ:** I didn't look at it. It only defines which "credible sources" can be used if Wikipedia isn't available.

**Latest news**
- **Oct 14:** NHC was issuing advisories on Tropical Storm Trudy… EP212026. Trudy was the 21st eastern Pacific system and the 19th name on the eastern Pacific list.
- **Oct 18 (Ryan Maue):** his headline reads "NE Pacific Hurricane Season: YTD: 22 Named Storms, ACE = 343". 22 total minus Trudy's 19 eastern Pacific names suggests about 3 central Pacific names, but that's my own arithmetic and I haven't confirmed it. He also wrote that Hurricane Trudy is about to rapidly collapse and become a remnant low. The Google DeepMind ensemble put the median peak of next system — Vance around 110 knots, which would be a major hurricane. AI models show Hurricane Vance forms off the coast of Mexico and drifts northward.
- **Oct 19 (FOX Weather):** the system will likely be named Vance as the first V-named storm from the East Pacific since 2018. Models disagree on landfall: AI models lean toward Baja California, while traditional models indicate a direct impact along Colima, Jalisco and Nayarit earlier next week.
- **About 25 days ago:** Cyclocane listed a 90% chance of eastern Pacific formation, with the next name Vance. That's an old snapshot.
- **No central Pacific storms** turned up in my searches for the coming days. The next names on the eastern Pacific list are Vance, Winnie, Xavier, Yolanda and Zeke.

**Forecasts and base rates**
- **Preseason forecasts:** SMN predicted 18–21 named storms. NOAA predicted 15–22 named storms, citing a strong El Niño. The season has already reached or passed the top of both ranges.
- **Long-term numbers:** average 15 (1991–2020); record 27 in 1992; record low 8 in 2010.
- **Late-season activity:** Late October often brings 0–2 more storms. In 2025, the season ended at 20 storms, and the last storm, Sonia, dissipated on October 28. In 2014, Vance originated from a trough... south-southeast of the Gulf of Tehuantepec and was named on Oct 30–31.

**Upshot**
- If nothing else formed, the answer would be about 22.
- If Vance forms as expected, it would be 23. That looks most likely.
- 24 or more would need another storm (Winnie, or a central Pacific system) by Oct 29. That's possible in a record El Niño year, but nothing points to it yet.
- **Caveats:** check the actual Wikipedia infobox, since the 22 comes from Maue rather than Wikipedia itself. A storm that crossed over from the Atlantic or a named subtropical storm could also change the count.
- **Prediction markets:** I didn't find any.

**Sources:**

- [2](https://www.va.gov/health/includes/NHC_Pacific_iframe.asp)

criterios: This question resolves to the cumulative number of named storms recorded in the 2026 Pacific hurricane season (the eastern North Pacific basin east of 140°W plus any that form in the central Pacific), as shown in the "Total storms" figure of the season-statistics infobox on the Wikipedia article "2026 Pacific hurricane season" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Pacific_hurricane_season) as of 23:59 UTC on October 29, 2026. A "named storm" is a tropical or subtropical cyclone that reached at least tropical-storm strength and was assigned a name by the National Hurricane Center or Central Pacific Hurricane Center. For example, if the infobox shows "Total storms: 23", this question resolves as 23. If the Wikipedia infobox is unavailable, the count published by the National Hurricane Center or [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions) covering the 2026 season will be used.
letra_pequena: The count reflects the cumulative season total as of 23:59 UTC on October 29, 2026, which includes all named storms that formed earlier in the 2026 season. Storms that form and are named at any point up to that time count, regardless of whether they are still active.
razonamientos:
(a) **Time left:** About 10 days, until 23:59 UTC on October 29.

(b) **If nothing changes:** The total remains **22 named storms**.

(c) **If the current trend continues:** The disturbance becomes Vance, bringing the total to **23**. Another storm before the deadline is possible.

(d) **Experts and markets:** The cited NHC outlook gave the disturbance a 60% chance of development over seven days as of October 16, and subsequent model discussion favored Vance forming. I found no usable prediction-market forecast for the final count.

(e) **Unexpected low scenario:** The disturbance fails to reach naming strength, leaving the count at **22**.

(f) **Unexpected high scenario:** Vance forms and two or more additional systems are named before October 29, bringing the count to **25 or more**.

The fractional percentiles below interpolate between possible integer counts; the resolved total will be a whole number.

Percentile 10: 22 named storms
Percentile 20: 22.3 named storms
Percentile 40: 22.8 named storms
Percentile 60: 23.2 named storms
Percentile 80: 23.8 named storms
Percentile 90: 24.5 named storms

**(a) Time left:** About 10 days, until 23:59 UTC on October 29, 2026.

**(b) If nothing changed:** 22 named storms. That is the year-to-date count Ryan Maue reported on Oct 18. Trudy has collapsed, and the Wikipedia infobox figure still needs to be checked directly.

**(c) If the current trend continued:** 23. The disturbance south of Mexico is widely expected to become Vance within days. NHC gave it 60% over 7 days on Oct 16. FOX Weather on Oct 19 said it will likely be named Vance. AI model ensembles show it becoming a strong hurricane. Given those signals and the 10 days left, Vance forming by Oct 29 looks roughly 85–90% likely.

**(d) Experts and markets:** I found no prediction markets. Forecasters and models (Maue, FOX Weather, the DeepMind ensemble) agree that Vance is coming soon. In active El Niño late seasons, late October usually brings 0–2 more storms. One more storm after Vance (Winnie) before Oct 29 is possible in a record season but not currently signalled. I put it at roughly 20%.

**(e) Low-outcome scenario:** The disturbance fails to organize, or only reaches tropical-depression strength. Shear or interaction with land prevents naming, and the count stays at 22.

**(f) High-outcome scenario:** Vance forms quickly, then a second system forms in the late-October El Niño pattern and is named Winnie. A system could also form in the central Pacific, or one could cross over from the Atlantic. Either path gives 24, or even 25. Wikipedia infobox quirks, such as counting depressions differently, add a little extra uncertainty.

My rough probabilities are:

| Count | Probability |
|---|---|
| 22 | ~11% |
| 23 | ~66% |
| 24 | ~19% |
| 25+ | ~4% |

(a) **Time left:** About 10 days, until 23:59 UTC on October 29.

(b) **If nothing changes:** The count remains 22 named storms.

(c) **If the current trend continues:** The likely formation of Vance brings the count to 23; another storm could bring it to 24.

(d) **Experts and markets:** The NHC gave the next disturbance a 60% development chance as of October 16, and subsequent reporting described Vance as likely. Preseason forecasts topped out near 22, but are less informative now. No useful prediction-market estimate was found.

(e) **Unexpected low outcome:** The disturbance fails to become a named storm, and no other system forms: 22.

(f) **Unexpected high outcome:** Several systems develop in quick succession, potentially including one in the central Pacific: 26 or more.
